Q2 2026 headline revenue growth is near-identical across the cohort — CPKC +12.6%, CN +11.3%, NSC +11.4%, UNP +11.5% — because diesel moved for everyone; Union Pacific disclosed a 60% increase in average price per gallon in the quarter.

Like-for-like against CN: CN is the one peer reporting in Canadian dollars under U.S. GAAP, sharing CPKC's western Canadian grain, potash, coal and Vancouver intermodal exposure with no Mexican network. If a three-nation land bridge produces structural growth, it should appear as CPKC outgrowing CN on the non-bulk base. On matched H1 2026 baskets, CPKC's ton-miles excluding grain, potash, fertilizers and coal grew 1.3% against CN's 1.7% excluding grain-and-fertilizers and coal, while total ton-miles grew 2.8% against 4.0%.▪ On the single quarter the ordering reverses: Q2 2026 on the matched basket gives CPKC +3.6% against CN +3.1%. No three-nation premium is visible in the half-year ton-mile data.

Where the network outgrew its end market: automotive. Mexican light-vehicle exports rose 1.4% in H1 2026 and January-to-May production declined 0.09% (mexicobusiness.news, accessed 2026-09-21) [web], while CPKC automotive ton-miles rose 5.2% and revenue 8.4% with revenue per carload up 12% and carloads down 3.2%. The gain is length of haul, with Mexico to Canada replacing Mexico to Laredo. Length-of-haul extension is a finite reallocation of existing traffic onto longer single-line routings, and once a shipper's flow has moved, the increment is spent.

The synergy claim: Management reports revenue synergies reaching C$1.4–1.5bn exiting 2026, "more than a $300 million step-up" over 2025 (Q2 2026 call). Underlying H1 2026 revenue growth after removing fuel price and FX was C$214m, roughly C$430m annualised. A step-up above C$300m against that means claimed synergies account for about 70% of all underlying growth, leaving the non-synergy base under 1%.▪ The CMO also states that land-bridge revenue is spread roughly evenly across intermodal, energy and chemicals, automotive and grain, so grain-to-Mexico is counted inside the land-bridge synergy figure and inside the record-harvest volume. The two explanations describe the same tonnes, and neither can be added to the other.

Cyclical or secular

The base-business trend rate the merger was layered onto is visible in legacy CP's last six years. Ton-miles peaked at 154,378m in FY2019 and were 4.0% lower in FY2022, while revenue rose 13.1% over the same three years and fuel surcharge revenue rose C$839m, from C$464m in 2019 to C$1,303m in 2022. Over FY2016–FY2022 ton-miles compounded at 1.5% a year and revenue at 6.0%. That matches the wider industry, in which U.S. rail carloads peaked in 2014 and have declined since while intermodal recovered to near-record levels.

Two of the four demand groups are at cycle extremes at once and pulling in opposite directions. Grain is at a peak, with western Canadian production 23% above its five-year average in 2025. Coal is at a company-specific trough, with ton-miles down 20% in H1 2026 and Elk Valley Resources having cut 140 positions in 2025 on challenging market conditions (cbc.ca, accessed 2026-09-21) [web]. Merchandise is mid-cycle and tariff-impaired, with Q1 2026 forest products revenue down 14% on Canadian lumber tariffs and cross-border steel "still effectively shut off". Netting them, the headline 2.8% ton-mile growth in H1 2026 is a peak-grain figure offset by a trough-coal figure: normalising grain toward its five-year average would remove roughly 3–4 points of consolidated ton-mile growth [estimate: western Canadian production 23% above the five-year average; grain was 34,599m of 112,302m H1'26 ton-miles, and a reversion of half the excess removes about 4,000m ton-miles, 3.6% of the base], and normalising coal back toward FY2025 run-rates would add roughly 2 points.

What can change the slope

Trade policy: At the USMCA joint review on 2026-07-01 the United States declined to extend the agreement, converting it into an annual review process running until the parties agree or the agreement expires on 2036-07-01, and on 2026-07-20 the U.S. announced 50% duties on a range of Canadian goods effective 2026-08-19 (whitecase.com, accessed 2026-09-21) [web]. The mechanism is already visible in the disclosed lines before those measures took effect, and the August duties land entirely in Q3 2026, which CPKC has not yet reported.

Pipeline substitution: Trans Mountain's expansion entered service in May 2024 and reached full utilisation in June 2026, and crude by rail was 1.8% of Canadian crude exports in 2025. CPKC no longer discloses crude revenue separately, so the exposure cannot be sized from current filings. Q2 2026 energy and chemicals ton-miles rose 6% partly on higher DRU and conventional crude, which runs against a simple secular-decline view at CPKC specifically even while the national series declines. Both facts are in the record.

Ocean-alliance routing: The Gemini Cooperation was the named driver of FY2025 international intermodal growth at Vancouver and Saint John, and in Q2 2026 those two ports were named as the source of the decline. Alliance routing is decided annually by third parties and reversed a line's growth in a single quarter.▪

Truck conversion: MMX at roughly 70% capacity and the CSX-partnered SMX growing more than 30% quarter on quarter are the clearest new products. They are also small against the line: intermodal ton-miles grew 2% in H1 2026 in total and Q2 intermodal carloads declined 1%. Section 17's base case makes intermodal the fastest-growing line at 4.1% a year while Section 3 grades network effects as absent partly on that same Q2 decline. Both can hold only if domestic truck conversion compounds at roughly 7.4% a year while the international half stays flat, which is the assumption the model makes and the one Section 17 flags as weak.

What would show first: Ranked by how early each disclosed series moves: carloads against ton-miles, because the length-of-haul extension that produced all of H1 2026's ton-mile growth shows up as ton-miles rising while carloads decline, and carloads were already −0.8%; ton-miles excluding grain, which were −2.1% in H1 2026; freight revenue per ton-mile against the disclosed fuel-price and FX effects, which was approximately zero; intermodal carloads at the named international ports; coal carloads; locomotives in storage and freight-car utilisation, annually; and train miles against gross ton-miles. Land-bridge revenue, cumulative synergy revenue and any line-level margin appear only in management commentary, so the central growth claim cannot be checked against an audited series.

7. Critical points

1. The C$31bn paid for Kansas City Southern moved CPKC from the highest return on capital in the group to the lowest, and three years of operating improvement have closed about a fifth of the gap. Return on invested capital was 15.0% in FY2019 and 14.9% in FY2020, two to four points above the five-peer mean. It is 6.0% in FY2025, 5.2 points below that mean, last of six, and below the Surface Transportation Board's 10.68% determination of the industry cost of capital for 2024.▪ Excluding C$21,347m of KCS goodwill and acquired intangibles the figure is 8.8%. The gap has narrowed 0.8 points over two years. The closest precedent in the class is BNSF, revalued by Berkshire's 2010 purchase, which has not returned to its pre-acquisition return level in sixteen years and peaked 4 points below its pre-deal mean.

2. Half of the freight-revenue growth since the merger is a record harvest, and the 2025 crop was 16% above its five-year average. Grain supplied C$470m of the C$913m of freight revenue growth from FY2024 to the twelve months ended June 2026 and 74% of the H1 2026 increase. Canadian principal field crop production of 107.0 Mt in 2025 was an all-time record, 16.2% above the 2020–2024 average. Canadian-origin grain is half the line, so a Canadian crop returning to its five-year mean removes about 7% of the grain line, roughly C$225m of revenue and C$70–100m of operating income at the constructed 31–44% contribution margin. Statistics Canada's September 2026 estimate has already softened the reversion: prairie wheat at 36.1 Mt is 10.9% below 2025 and still above the five-year average, and canola at 22.1 Mt is 0.8% below.

3. Realized price and renewal price are different numbers, and the published yield series uses the one that is not growing. Management has described renewals at or above the top of its 3–4% outlook on five consecutive calls. Stripping fuel surcharge and the disclosed FX effect, core freight revenue per ton-mile rose 0.7% in FY2025 and 0.4% in H1 2026, while core revenue per carload rose 1.2% and 4.1%. The 3.7-point gap in the half is length of haul, up 3.7%. At the FY2025 marginal ex-fuel cost of 1.43 cents per ton-mile against a 5.99-cent core yield, each point of length-of-haul extension adds roughly C$130m of revenue at about a 76% contribution, and the extension is a one-time reallocation of existing traffic onto longer single-line routings.

4. Fuel surcharge makes FY2026 revenue growth look like recovery and FY2026 margin look like deterioration, and both are the same accounting. Surcharge revenue enters at a 100% incremental operating ratio. In Q2 2026 revenue rose C$465m of which C$258m was surcharge, while fuel expense rose C$213m; recomputing the reported operating ratio with both increments removed gives 63.5% against 63.7%, a 20bp improvement in place of the 90bp deterioration reported. Ex-surcharge operating margin was 41.7% in both Q2 2026 and Q2 2025. Three of the five other North American Class Is moved the same direction on the same mechanism in the same quarter.

5. Volume dominates the forward earnings range, because only 40–55% of an average cost dollar recurs on the next ton-mile. FY2025 organic operating expense rose C$186m on 7,962m additional ton-miles, 2.34 cents per incremental ton-mile against a 4.32-cent average and 1.43 against 3.53 excluding fuel. In the forward model a 1.5-point move either way in ton-mile growth over 2027–2032 is worth C$2,104m of the FY2032 operating-income range, roughly 1.4 times what a 1-point move in yield is worth and twenty times the whole span of headcount elasticity. It works in both directions: in FY2021 and FY2022 ex-fuel revenue grew C$47m and C$51m while ex-fuel operating income declined C$141m and C$99m, because ton-miles declined 4.0% over four years while ex-fuel operating expense per ton-mile rose 19%.

6. Consensus asks for three consecutive years of operating-ratio improvement at about 145bp a year; no Class I has improved four years running from a sub-65% base and the current half is going the other way. The consensus path implies 60.5% in 2026, 58.3% in 2027 and 56.5% in 2028. Management's own stated pace is 100bp a year. H1 2026 core adjusted operating ratio was 62.3% against 61.6%, 70bp worse, and Q2 was 90bp worse. Across 46 three-year windows in the Class I reference class beginning from a sub-65% ratio, the median outcome was 120bp of deterioration, six windows beat 340bp of improvement and one beat 630bp. Counting runs of consecutive improving years from a sub-65% base across the class since 1995: ten single years, three two-year runs, three three-year runs, none of four. Each 100bp of operating ratio on consensus CY2028 revenue is C$186m, roughly C$0.18 of EPS.

7. Shareholder returns have exceeded free cash flow since the buyback restarted, and leverage is moving away from the stated target. FY2025 returned C$4,738m against free cash flow of C$2,169m; H1 2026 returned C$2,371m against C$1,267m. The gaps were funded with net new borrowing of C$1,527m and C$1,208m, the Panama sale proceeds and a cash drawdown. Disclosed adjusted net debt to adjusted EBITDA went 3.0x at 2025-06-30, 3.1x at year end and 3.2x at 2026-06-30 against a 2.75x target on the September 2026 deck, and the 2023 Investor Day target was 2.5x flat from 2024 through 2028. Deleveraging since 2021 came from the denominator: net debt of C$23,004m in 2025 is above the C$20,058m peak of 2021, while EBITDA grew from C$4,017m to C$7,628m.

8. Coal is 6.8% of revenue and cost about two points of group volume growth in 2026 because one counterparty's pits and one port programme set the tonnage. Q2 2026 coal revenue declined 18% and ton-miles 29%; H1 revenue declined 15% on ton-miles down 20%. Glencore's own half-year report confirms the mine-side cause and cut 2026 guidance from 30–34 Mt to 30–32 Mt. CN's coal revenue declined 5.3% in H1 2026 from the same southeast British Columbia basin against CPKC's 15.2%, so CPKC's single-origin exposure is three times the effect at its nearest comparable.▪ Creel: "That 4% I talked about, if not for coal, if it were normalized at 6% RTM growth."

9. The pending UP–NS decision sets CPKC's Chicago and Kansas City gateway economics and cannot be sized from any CPKC disclosure. Ten years of 10-Ks disaggregate revenue by commodity and by country and never by connection or gateway. The only disclosed number is the cost of fighting: C$13m in Q1 2026 and C$14m in Q2, C$27m in the half, C$21m after tax and two cents of diluted EPS. The statutory decision deadline is 2027-08-28, inside the forecast window, and the 2026-11-18 filing is the first public document in which CPKC has to state its own exposure.

10. Mexico is 18% of revenue and roughly 20% of net property, and no profitability figure for it exists. Mexican revenue was C$2,711m in FY2025 against C$11,326m of properties and operating-lease right-of-use assets. It operates on a concession to June 2047 with exclusive freight rights only through 2037, a 1.25%-of-gross-revenue duty, maximum rates registered with ATTRAPI, and an obligation to return the assets with no compensation if the concession is terminated. The C$9,176m of concession rights inside the purchase price allocation is amortized over a 74-year assumption that extends ten years past the exclusivity. A 2014 Mexican tax assessment stood at Ps.6,667m (C$540m) at 2026-06-30, and CPKC registered an ICSID arbitration against Mexico under the CPTPP on 2026-04-27 after four years of domestic process.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"We continue to do what we said we would do." The phrase appears in the Q4 2024 and Q3 2025 earnings releases, and Creel repeated the substance at Laguna on 2026-09-17: "we're clearly in line to deliver on the guidance that we've given for the year." Across six closed years with a numeric annual earnings guide the initial guide was met twice, in 2019 and 2024, and cut three times, in 2020, 2021 and 2023; in 2025 the cut guide was also missed. Average shortfall against the initial-guide midpoint is about two percentage points. FY2025 delivered +8% against a guide of 12–18% cut to 10–14% in April and reaffirmed twice after the cut, including by the CFO on 2025-10-29 with the year five-sixths done: "we are very confident, we'll be able to achieve at least 10% EPS growth for the year. So we're not backing off of that with 8 or 9 weeks here left to go." The volume record is worse: CPKC has not delivered a mid- or high-single-digit ton-mile year against a mid- or high-single-digit ton-mile guide anywhere in the eight-year window.

"The only piece of the equation that isn't exactly sort of how we thought it would play out was sort of that organic growth" (Brooks, Wells Fargo, 2026-06-10); "we haven't had the 3% to 4%. It's been around 1%. But we've overachieved on price" (Velani, UBS, 2025-12-02). Two of the three legs have underdelivered, against the one Brooks names. FY2025 revenue ex-surcharge rose 5.4% against ton-mile growth of 3.8%, so realized yield added about 1.7 points against a stated 3–4% price leg. In H1 2026 the same arithmetic turns negative: ex-surcharge revenue rose 2.4% on ton-mile growth of 2.8%, a realized yield contribution of about −0.4 points. Same-store renewal price and realized yield are different measures and the revenue build treats them as one.

"We've got a product that can't be replicated in the marketplace" (Brooks, Q2 2026 call). Falcon Premium, a CN, Union Pacific and Ferromex interline Canada–U.S.–Mexico intermodal service, was announced about a week after CPKC was formed. BNSF and J.B. Hunt moved their Mexico intermodal service from CPKC's Laredo routing to Ferromex via Eagle Pass effective 1 January 2024, on a routing they state is a day faster. CN gained operating rights over Union Pacific between Memphis and Eagle Pass in July 2026, and those rights do not depend on the merger. Management's own answer narrows the claim usefully: the CN routing runs "over Chicago… they got to go east to come back West", which is a route-mile disadvantage from western Canadian origins and no disadvantage from Chicago or the U.S. Southeast. Both statements hold for different origins.

"Return to double-digit Core adjusted ROIC" by 2028 (September 2026 deck, slide 22, footnoted to the 2023 Investor Day). FY2025 core adjusted ROIC is about 6.5% on the reconstruction in Section 3, or 9.5% excluding goodwill and intangibles; CPKC's own reinstated figure in the January 2026 year-end release is 6.9% against 6.7% for FY2024. Reaching 10% on an unchanged capital base requires core adjusted operating income near C$9.3bn, about 50% above FY2025, or roughly 100bp of improvement a year for three years against the 20bp added in 2025.▪ Adjusted ROIC appeared seven times in the FY2022 10-K and has appeared in none of the FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 10-Ks; the last value in a 10-K was 6.9% for FY2022, against 8.2% for 2021, 16.7% for 2020 and 16.9% for 2019. The measure was also removed from the long-term incentive plan with the 2022 grant and has not returned in five grant years. Velani's own explanation, at Scotiabank on 2025-11-18: "saying you're going to raise 7% to 7.5% is too tight a range to really measure and put compensation towards."

"We're going to exit this year about $1.5 billion of revenue synergies" (Creel, Morgan Stanley Laguna, 2026-09-17) against a September 2021 commitment of "US$1 billion in annualized EBITDA synergies" within three years of closing. The deck footnote states the synergy estimates are in U.S. dollars, and the components were US$820m of EBITDA growth from market opportunities plus US$180m of cost and efficiency improvements. What has been reported since 2024 is Canadian-dollar revenue. C$1.5bn of revenue at incremental EBITDA margins of 50–75% produces C$750m–1,125m, or US$545–815m, against the US$820m market-opportunity target plus US$180m of cost synergies, so the outcome reaches plan only at the top of that range▪ [estimate: the 50% floor is CPKC's own FY2025 EBITDA margin; the 75% ceiling is the incremental margin in the March 2021 deck]. The unit has also been relabelled twice in the other direction: Creel at Citi on 2026-02-18 said the original US$1bn was "revenue synergies, not EBITDA synergies", and Velani at BofA on 2026-05-13 applied the EBITDA label to the current number.

The synergy run rate cannot be added to the revenue build. A C$1.2bn synergy run rate exiting 2025 and C$1.4–1.5bn exiting 2026 stands against roughly C$1.0bn of core organic revenue increase over the two years to FY2025, once the disclosed C$1,375m KCS-acquisition increment, the C$140m surcharge decline and the C$252m of favourable FX are removed [estimate: FY2023 reported revenue plus the FY2024 10-K's disclosed acquisition-period increment as the full-year 2023 equivalent]. Velani flagged the definitional problem himself at the 2023 Investor Day: "at some point, the synergies it becomes, is it base growth, is it synergies, right?"

"Best margins in the industry" (Velani, 2023 Investor Day). FY2025 GAAP operating ratios: UNP 59.8%, CN 61.9%, CPKC 62.8%, NSC 64.2%, BNSF 65.6%, CSX 67.9%. CPKC's core adjusted 59.9% would match UNP's GAAP figure, and the exclusion that produces it is KCS purchase-accounting amortization recurring over the acquired assets' useful lives — 250bp of the 290bp gap, every year, with a further 40bp of acquisition-related costs and a new C$27m of STB advisory costs in H1 2026.▪

"Mid-50s operating ratio." Creel at Morgan Stanley Laguna on 2022-09-15: "obviously, I'm not going to tell you don't assume, we're going to get to the mid-50s. We will." Velani at BofA on 2026-05-13: "I think the goal is not to get to mid-50s. The goal is to focus on what we think is a true core metric of shareholder return is return on invested capital." The commitment was repeated for five years, was not reached, and was replaced with a measure CPKC does not report in its 10-K.▪

"More than double our EPS" from 2023 to 2028. Velani's June 2023 statement was against an implied 2023 base of C$3.95–4.00, so more than C$7.90; the printed FY2023 base was C$3.84, so the doubling is C$7.68. Delivered: C$4.25 in 2024, C$4.61 in 2025, a two-year compound rate of 9.6%. Consensus for CY2028 is C$6.837, 11% below the C$7.68 version and 13.5–14.5% below the C$7.90–8.00 version, and reaches the doubling only in 2029 on the C$7.800 CY2029 mean.▪ Management last volunteered the target in June 2023 and has since answered only when asked, with the answer conditioned: "Certainly, mid-teens kind of EPS growth is certainly achievable in a better macro environment."

"Target leverage 2.75x." The 2023 Investor Day showed a path to 2.5x held flat from 2024 through 2028. The target was raised to 2.75x before the buyback restarted, stated first at Citi on 2025-02-18 and printed on the October 2025 and September 2026 decks. The disclosed ratio moved from 3.0x at 2025-06-30 to 3.2x at 2026-06-30, 0.45x above the target and widening, while adjusted net debt grew C$3,302m over those twelve months against C$356m of adjusted EBITDA growth. Without the C$4,190m of repurchases in that window, adjusted net debt would have been roughly C$21.6bn and the ratio about 2.7x.

"Zero goodwill impairment shows the price was justified." CPKC has one reportable segment and the goodwill note refers to a single reporting unit, so the annual 1 October test compares the entire railroad's fair value with its entire carrying value. Market capitalization of roughly C$107,000m at 2026-09-21 against total equity of roughly C$48,000m means an impairment would require the whole enterprise to be worth less than book. The C$17,632m of goodwill would survive a very large disappointment in the KCS assets specifically.

What CPKC is today was set by five events.

  • The Norfolk Southern failure, 2015–2016. CP was willing to run leverage near 3x and spend C$2,787m of buyback in one year while bidding for a competitor. When the bid failed it did not redirect the money into larger buybacks; buybacks stepped down 86% to C$381m by 2017 while leverage went from 2.9x to 2.3x, and capex rose 40% from the 2016 trough. Revenue then compounded 9.0% a year to 2019.
  • The Harrison-to-Creel handover, January 2017. Creel described the change directly: "we had a mandate to fix the company… as we shifted in 2017, and I took over as the CEO, I had a mandate with my team to grow the company." Adjusted return on capital improved 290bp over the three Creel years despite higher capital spend. The margin franchise survived the founder's exit and the growth franchise was built on top of it.
  • Kansas City Southern, 2021–2023. Revenue roughly doubled and workload rose 48%, and the operating ratio went the other way, from 57.1% in 2020 to 62.8% reported and 59.9% core adjusted in 2025. Return on invested capital went from 16.7% disclosed in 2020 to about 7% rebuilt on the same formula for 2025. The stated synergy number rose three times before closing and again after.
  • The 2025 guidance miss. CP or CPKC cut its published volume guidance mid-year in 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2025, and in the first three it still delivered the reduced earnings guide by pulling cost. 2025 broke that pattern: ton-mile growth of 4% came in near plan and core adjusted EPS grew 8% against a 10–14% commitment made in April and reaffirmed in October, with the gap arising below the operating line on tax and interest.
  • The capital-return restart, 2025. Four years of zero buyback and a dividend frozen at C$0.760 ended with C$3,942m of repurchases, a 15% dividend increase and a further 17.5% increase in April 2026, funded at the margin with debt.

Margin and capital commitments are delivered and volume forecasts are not: the original volume outlook came in low in all six disclosed forecast years. Disclosure also narrows when a number turns — Adjusted ROIC was reported every year from 2012 through 2022 and stopped after a print of 6.9%; the 10-K's outlook-versus-actual table ran in FY2019, FY2020 and FY2021 and stopped; the dividend payout target appeared ten times in the FY2021 10-K and not at all in FY2024 or FY2025; and the adjusted net debt to EBITDA reconciliation moved out of the 10-K and into the quarterly earnings release.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

Who runs it

Officer Age Role At CPKC since In role since

John Brooks 55 EVP and Chief Marketing Officer 2007 Feb 2019

Creel is the longest-tenured Class I CEO. Three of the five came from CN or KCS, so the operating philosophy traces to Hunter Harrison's CN and to the KCS network Redd ran, and no external hire has entered the top five roles. One substantive departure: John Orr, KCS's operations head, became CPKC's Chief Transformation Officer on the control date, received an annual grant plus a one-time deferred-share award in lieu of a merger-agreement cash payment, and left for Norfolk Southern eleven months later; CPKC "agreed to waive enforcement of Mr. Orr's non-competition provision solely with respect to his employment with NS" (FY2023 10-K/A, Item 11).

Pay design and what it measures

Ninety-three percent of the CEO's 2025 target direct compensation is variable, and long-term incentive splits 60% performance share units and 40% options. The units cliff-vest at three years and pay in cash; options vest over four years with a seven-year term. The comparator group is five Class I railroads plus 14 capital-intensive North American companies, eleven Canadian and eight U.S., unchanged from 2024. Governance features constrain the design: a no-fault Dodd-Frank clawback plus a separate senior-executive policy, anti-hedging and anti-pledging policies, two-year non-competes on all named officers, double-trigger option vesting, and no tax gross-up on any termination benefit. Option dilution is 0.58% of shares with a three-year burn rate of 0.09%, 0.09% and 0.11%.

Short-term incentive measure Weight 2025 threshold / target / max 2025 result Score
Operating ratio 35% 61.3% / 60.4% / 59.3% 60.4% 100%
Operating income 35% C$6,024m / C$6,216m / C$6,528m C$6,112m 73%
FRA train accident frequency 15% 1.35 / 1.21 / 0.99 0.85 200%
FRA personal injury frequency 15% 1.14 / 1.08 / 1.00 0.92 200%
Corporate factor 121%

Safety supplied 60 of the 121 points. The 2025 personal-injury maximum of 1.00 was set above the 2024 actual of 0.95, so a 200% score required only that frequency not deteriorate by about 5%, and the train-accident scale was left unchanged from 2024. The financial half scored 87% on a weighted basis. The board capped Creel's individual factor at 100% "recognizing that overall corporate financial results, while strong, fell short of expectations", and applied the same cap to 30 officers. The plan can also pay close to nothing: the 2022 corporate factor was 29%.

On the long-term side, adjusted ROIC was the financial measure at a 70% weight through the 2021 grant and was removed for the 2022 grant because "the KCS transaction-related impacts such as timing uncertainty and purchase accounting implications make goal setting and measuring ROIC performance challenging". It has not returned in five grant years. The 2023 grant, which vested 2025-12-31, paid 91% of target: three-year cumulative free cash flow of C$9,556m against a C$9,150m target scored 151% on a 60% weight, while total shareholder return landed in the 11th percentile of the S&P/TSX 60 and the 5th percentile of the S&P 500 Industrials, scoring zero on both 20% weights. Five-year cumulative shareholder return to 2025-12-31 was 19% in Canadian dollars and 10% in U.S. dollars against 111% for the S&P/TSX Composite and 96% for the S&P 500; named-officer total direct compensation was 15% above the 2021 level.

About 64% of the long-term award, options plus relative shareholder return, is tied to the share price, and that portion behaved as designed: Creel's realizable value on each of the last three awards is roughly two-thirds of grant value. The financial measures are absolute dollars. Operating income and cumulative free cash flow both rise when an acquisition adds revenue and assets, and no measure in the current plan divides return by capital. Two design features run the other way: free cash flow is struck after capital expenditure, so the C$3.1bn of 2025 capital spend reduced the measured result, and the 2022 grant's net-debt-to-EBITDA modifier was written to pay up to 1.5x on reaching 2.5x by dates running to 2024-09-30, was missed, and paid nothing.

Support for the pay design declined and stayed down: say-on-pay was 92.52% for in 2022, 94.05% in 2024, 87.74% in 2025 and 87.48% in 2026, while the lowest director result in 2026 was 95.84%, so the dissent is specific to pay. In June 2025 the board added C$1,851,971 of performance units to Creel's 2025 award after concluding "the CEO's pay was not as competitively positioned relative to peers as intended", in the same year it capped his individual rating for performance below expectations. Both decisions cite 2025 performance.

Insider ownership

Directly held shares across all 24 executive officers and directors total 280,068 against 897,958,953 outstanding, 0.031% of the company. Seven of the twelve incumbent non-CEO directors hold no common shares and meet the guideline entirely through deferred share units, which settle in cash and are excluded from the beneficial-ownership table. Creel shows ownership of 14.57x salary of which 63% is cash-settled units; his direct holding is 99,898 shares against 1,527,958 shares issuable on options exercisable within 60 days. TCI Fund Management's 6.19% from a 2024 Schedule 13G/A is the only disclosed holder above 5%.

CPKC officers are exempt from Section 16, so no Forms 3, 4 or 5 exist. EDGAR lists ten Form 144 notices for CIK 0000016875 between 2023-05-10 and 2024-01-10. Four have been examined in detail, each a Keith Creel same-day option exercise and sale through the same broker: 39,318 shares on 2023-09-11 for US$3,004,682, 39,318 on 2023-11-13 for US$2,862,350, 39,318 on 2023-12-11 for US$2,865,889 and 78,636 on 2024-01-10 for US$6,171,353, totalling 196,590 shares for about US$14.9m. Six further notices are in the record. Canadian-market transactions file to SEDI and are not on EDGAR, so this is the U.S. leg only. No open-market purchase by any insider appears in the EDGAR record.

Capex took 53.7% of ten-year operating cash flow, M&A 35.5%, buybacks 26.3% and dividends 14.8%, 130% in total. The 30-point excess was funded by C$7,758m of net new long-term debt, C$1,103m of net short-term borrowing, C$1,110m of asset sales and a C$466m cash drawdown. Cumulative free cash flow was C$16,338m and cumulative dividends plus buybacks C$14,497m, 89% of it, with lopsided timing: 2016–2020 returned C$7,129m against C$5,384m of free cash flow, 2021–2024 returned C$2,630m against C$8,785m, and 2025 alone returned C$4,738m against C$2,169m.

The buyback record has one hard fact in it. The 2014–2020 programmes bought 226.4m split-adjusted shares for C$10,173m at an average of C$44.94, about 26% of the base. The KCS acquisition then issued 262.6m shares at C$89.34. The 2025 and H1 2026 programmes have since retired 53.9m of those, 21% of the issuance, at C$107.61 and C$117.18. CPKC spent C$10.2bn retiring shares and four years later issued more shares than it had retired, at roughly double the price, and is now buying them back at 2.4x the original average cost.

Price sensitivity inside a programme is close to nil, and the mechanism is disclosed. Each programme is a normal course issuer bid with a cap in shares: 37.3 million in 2025 and approximately 44.9 million in 2026, each expiring inside about twelve months. A fixed share authorization spends more dollars when the price is higher. The share-weighted average cost was C$107.61 in 2025 against C$107.92 as the unweighted average of active months, an advantage of 0.3%, worth about C$12m across 37.3m shares; for H1 2026 the advantage is 0.1%. Velani described the constraint directly: "you can't get too cute on some of those things, especially when you have a 45 million share authorization."

Capital spending is 92% renewal and rolling stock. Within the C$1,736m track-and-roadway line in FY2025, C$1,500m renewed depleted assets and C$236m went to network improvements and growth, 13.6% of that line. Rolling stock tripled to C$930m on Tier 4 locomotives, which CPKC describes as fleet efficiency and reliability, not capacity addition. Against the 2023 Investor Day envelope of C$2.6–2.8bn a year, still printed on the September 2026 deck, actual spend was C$2,499m in 2023, C$2,863m in 2024 and C$3,140m in 2025; the FY2025 figure exceeded the top of the range by 12%, attributed by Velani to a Q4 pull-forward of maintenance projects, and 2026 is guided to C$2.65bn.

Per-share outcomes run behind enterprise outcomes at every step. From FY2019 to FY2025, revenue rose 93.5% in total and 47.0% per share; operating income 79.5% and 36.4%; diluted EPS 28.7%; free cash flow 61.5% and 22.7%. The diluted share count rose 31.7% over those six years. The two gaps between operating income and cash are net interest expense, which rose from C$448m to C$876m, and current income tax of C$1,174m in 2025. Dividends declared per share were C$0.760 in each of 2021 through 2024, then C$0.874 in 2025 and a further 17.5% quarterly increase in April 2026; on FY2025 core adjusted EPS the payout is 19.0%, below both stated targets — "closer to 25%, 30%" on the Q4 2024 call and "20% to 30%" on the Q1 2025 call, thirteen weeks apart.

The 2023 Investor Day's free-cash-conversion target of about 90% of core adjusted income is still printed on the current deck. Reconstructing it on the company's own Q3 2023 construction gives about 66% for FY2024 and about 51% for FY2025 [estimate: operating cash flow less investing cash flow, adjusted for the FX effect on cash, acquisition-related costs and the Panama sale proceeds, over core adjusted diluted EPS times diluted shares; range 50–68% depending on the treatment of adjusting items]. Averaging 90% across 2024–2028 from those two years requires about 111% in each of 2026, 2027 and 2028, meaning free cash above core adjusted income in each year.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

The same gap applies here: no disclosure separates the acquired network's revenue or margin after 2023, so what the Mexican and U.S. assets earn is unknown and the judgment uses consolidated per-share and return outcomes.

CPKC executed one transformational deal cleanly and paid a price it has not yet earned back. Kansas City Southern was integrated on schedule, has produced no goodwill impairment, no regulator-forced divestiture and no restatement of the purchase price allocation beyond C$141m of measurement-period adjustments, and systems integration finished in 2025. On price and per-share arithmetic the record is weaker. CP paid roughly 23x KCS's trailing EBITDA using stock and cash the market valued at roughly 17x, raised its own bid by US$25 per KCS share after Canadian National intervened, and spent a net US$700m on break fees to prevail.▪ Aggregate core adjusted income compounded at 13.3% a year from 2021 to 2025, matching legacy CP's pre-deal rate; adjusted diluted earnings per share compounded at 5.2% against 13.3% in the four years to 2021, and the eight-point difference went to the 34.3% increase in the diluted share count.▪ Over the same window Union Pacific, CSX and Norfolk Southern each shrank their diluted counts by 12–19%. The pre-KCS record is thinner: a C$185m write-off of the Powder River Basin build option in 2012, a C$435m impairment in 2013 ahead of the DM&E West sale, and a hostile approach to Norfolk Southern abandoned thirteen days after filing a definitive contested proxy.

Price paid against price traded: On an enterprise value of about US$31bn, which follows from the US$300 per share at announcement plus assumed KCS debt and does not appear on the announcement deck, the deal is 22.8x KCS's FY2020 EBITDA of US$1,361m and 11.8x FY2020 sales. CP's own enterprise value on the 2021-08-09 reference date was about C$71,200m — 667.1m shares at the C$91.50 close plus roughly C$10,200m of adjusted net debt implied by the disclosed 2.5x leverage — against FY2020 EBITDA of C$4,090m, so 17.4x and 9.2x sales [estimate: market capitalization from the deck's own reference price and pre-issuance share count; net debt implied by the disclosed leverage ratio]. Both figures use each company's own reported operating income and depreciation on a trailing FY2020 basis. The gap is about five and a half turns.

Purchase price allocation: Goodwill of C$17,632m equals 46.2% of the C$38,171m control-date accounting consideration, attributed to future synergies and an acquired assembled workforce, assigned entirely to the rail transportation segment, and not deductible for tax. Inside Properties are Mexican concession rights and related assets at a provisional fair value of C$9,176m, amortized over the shorter of asset lives and the concession term including one renewal, a 74-year assumption. Intangibles of C$3,022m are contracts and customer relationships amortized over nine to 22 years plus indefinite-lived U.S. trackage rights and the KCS brand. The C$7,175m remeasurement loss on derecognising the previously held equity investment is not an overpayment marker: the same entry recognised a C$7,832m deferred tax recovery on derecognising the outside-basis deferred tax liability, leaving a net C$657m credit, and both items make FY2023 GAAP pre-tax income, effective tax rate and net income unusable without adjustment.

Integration cost has not closed. Acquisition-related costs excluded from core adjusted results total C$1,143m: C$599m (2021), C$123m (2022), C$201m (2023), C$112m (2024), C$72m (2025) and C$36m in H1 2026. The FY2025 10-K states CPKC "continues to expect to incur acquisition-related costs beyond the year of acquisition", five years after announcement. A separate exclusion appeared in 2026 for STB advisory costs on the UP–NS review. Purchase accounting is a permanent wedge: 250bp of the 290bp between the FY2025 GAAP and core adjusted operating ratios.

Synergy delivery against the stated measure is covered as a pressure test in Section 8. The mix has shifted: crude-by-rail, one of the named pillars of the 2021 case, has been written off by the CEO, while the Canada–U.S.–Mexico land bridge grew from roughly C$100m in 2023 to over C$600m with C$1bn targeted. Neither component's original size was separately disclosed at announcement, so the two cannot be netted from the filings.

The two bids made opposite cases. For Norfolk Southern, 72% of the claimed US$1.8bn was operational self-help CP said it would impose on the target and 28% was combination synergy. For KCS, US$820m of the US$1,000m was revenue from market opportunities on the combined network and only US$180m was cost. The half of the KCS case that depends on winning new freight is the half that has slipped. Creel on what happens next if the industry consolidates further: "I'm adamantly opposed to additional rail consolidation… But if it's forced, we're not going to stand still… I can make a value proposition case with a host of partners" (Q2 2026 call).

Secured and first-charge obligations total roughly C$134m of C$23,291m gross, about 0.6%: two Federal Railroad Administration RRIF loans secured by 30 locomotives and by Mexrail's per-car bridge fees at Laredo, finance leases secured by C$100m of assets, and C$47m of perpetual 4% debenture stock authorized by an 1889 Act of Parliament that is a first charge over the whole undertaking. Canadian Pacific Railway Company is the issuer and CPKC guarantees on an unsecured basis; CPRC's own subsidiaries do not guarantee, so bondholders are structurally subordinated to liabilities at the Mexican concession subsidiary and the U.S. KCS estate. In practice C$19,811m of the C$19,948m of consolidated long-term debt is at CPRC and CPKC.

Weighted-average cost of debt = each instrument's stated coupon weighted by its balance-sheet amount at 2025-12-31. The two ranged rows use midpoints and together are C$170m, so the choice moves the answer by under a basis point. The commercial paper leg uses the disclosed weighted-average rate of 4.02%.

The principal-weighted coupon is 3.88% across C$23,291m of gross debt: 3.87% on C$22,052m of notes, debentures and RRIF loans, 4.00% on the perpetuals and 4.02% on commercial paper. Fixed-rate only, excluding commercial paper, is 3.87% on C$22,126m. The cash rate is close: reported net interest expense was C$876m in FY2025 and interest paid C$863m, against C$904m of computed coupon, and the roughly C$30m gap is interest income netted, capitalized interest and the discount. Floating exposure is the commercial paper leg alone, C$1,165m or 5.0% of gross debt at year end and C$1,461m or 5.8% at 2026-06-30, on which the commercial paper rate moved from 4.02% to 2.70% over the half.

Maturity wall and refinancing cost

Annual principal repayments excluding finance leases: 2026 C$3,228m, 2027 C$7m, 2028 C$1,893m, 2029 C$990m, 2030 C$1,514m, thereafter C$16,189m. The 2026 figure includes C$1,165m of commercial paper that rolls at under 90 days, so term maturities were C$2,063m, of which C$684m was repaid in H1 2026 and the remainder is the US$1,000m 1.75% notes due December 2026. The 2027 maturity is C$7m.

The C$5,694m of term notes still outstanding and maturing 2026–2030 has a weighted-average coupon of 2.87%. New-issue coupons in 2025 and 2026 ran 4.00% to 5.50% across seven issues. Refinancing that block at 4.0% adds C$65m of annual interest, at 4.5% C$93m, at 5.0% C$121m and at 5.5% C$150m — 7% to 17% of FY2025 net interest expense, phased over five years [estimate: bucket coupon weighted by 2025 balance-sheet amounts; new-money rate taken from the range of actual 2025–2026 issue coupons]. The market prices this already: debt with a book value of C$23,686m was worth C$22,182m at 2026-06-30, a 6.3% discount, wider than the 5.8% discount at year end. Item 7A discloses that a one-point decrease in rates would raise the fair value of the debt by about C$1.8bn, which implies modified duration near 8.7 years.

Liquidity, covenants and ratings

Cash was C$366m at 2026-06-30 against an undrawn US$2.2bn revolving facility with 15 institutions in two tranches, extended in July 2026 to June 2028 and June 2031. The commercial paper programme maximum was raised from US$1.5bn to US$2.2bn on 2026-03-27 with the addition of a Canadian-dollar tranche, and US$1,028m was outstanding; the programme is fully backstopped by the revolver, which makes the C$1,461m balance a pricing exposure while the revolver stands. Letters of credit drawn were C$83m of C$300m available.

The credit agreements require a financial covenant that CPKC states it satisfied at both year ends. Neither the test nor its level appears in the 10-K and has not since at least FY2020, and the September 2021 amendment that provided two years of covenant flexibility for the acquisition financing has lapsed, so headroom cannot be measured from the filings. Ratings recovered the notch the acquisition cost: Moody's moved Baa1 to Baa2 during 2021 and back to Baa1 stable in Q1 2025, while S&P held BBB+ throughout and moved the outlook to positive in Q4 2025.

Leases and pension

Leases are immaterial at C$437m of total liabilities, 1.9% of gross debt, with total lease cost of C$153m in FY2025. Pension is not immaterial. The defined benefit plans held C$14,794m of assets against a C$4,974m surplus at 2025-12-31, and the balance-sheet pension asset of C$5,129m is 6.0% of total assets. Other components of net periodic benefit recovery were C$415m pre-tax in FY2025 and C$421m in the twelve months to 2026-06-30, against a 2024–2028 plan assumption of C$330–370m a year, so the plan is contributing above what the earnings target assumed. This is non-cash income equal to about 8% of FY2025 pre-tax profit, and it depends on an expected return on plan assets of 6.70% producing C$926m against C$488m of interest cost on the obligation. Employer defined-benefit contributions were C$13m against C$663m of benefits paid, so the plans fund themselves from asset returns and none of the surplus is distributable. Sensitivity runs both ways: 0.1 point of expected return moves other components by C$14m, and 0.1 point of discount rate moves the obligation by C$111–113m.

Share count and dilution

Stock-based compensation is almost entirely cash-settled, so it produces expense volatility and almost no shares. Gross issuance under option plans was 1.4m shares in each of 2024 and 2025, 0.15% of the opening count, and options outstanding are about 5.3m, 0.6% of shares. There is no convertible instrument and no preferred share outstanding. Expense ranged from C$35m (2017) to C$170m (2020) and was C$59m in FY2025, C$49m below FY2024; the FY2025 10-K attributes the change to "changes in payout rates, net of impacts from share price". Sensitivity roughly doubled inside 2026: every C$1.00 of share price moves the expense C$2.2m to C$2.4m at 2026-06-30 against C$1.3m to C$1.9m at 2025-12-31, and H1 2026 already recorded C$37m of share-price component. Canada levies a 2% tax on net repurchases, accrued at C$77m for 2025 and C$36m for H1 2026.

Net share count went 933.5m at 2024-12-31 to 879.1m at 2026-07-28, a 5.8% reduction; diluted weighted-average shares were 934.6m in FY2024, 917.1m in FY2025 and 887.1m in Q2 2026.

Peer leverage

Ratios are currency-neutral; net debt is from each company's 2026-06-30 balance sheet, CPKC on trailing-twelve-month EBITDA to that date and the peers on FY2025 operating income plus depreciation.

CPKC is the most levered of the five, and it and CN added debt over the first half of 2026 while the three U.S. roads did not. CPKC's EBITDA is also flattered relative to the peers by C$373m of KCS purchase-accounting amortization added back in EBITDA, where the equivalent economic cost is embedded in the peers' ordinary depreciation.

Structural risks, ranked by the size of the cash or covenant consequence

  1. Leverage is rising against a target it is not approaching. Disclosed adjusted net debt to adjusted EBITDA went 3.0x at 2025-06-30 to 3.2x at 2026-06-30 against a stated 2.75x on the same adjusted basis. The gap is a discretionary repurchase choice.
  2. The 2026–2030 wall reprices C$5,694m of 2.87% paper at the 4.00–5.50% coupons achieved in 2025 and 2026, C$65m to C$150m of incremental annual interest.
  3. Commercial paper reliance. C$1,461m outstanding against C$366m of cash, fully backstopped by the undrawn revolver.
  4. The covenant level is unpublished, with the disclosed leverage ratio at 3.2x and rising.
  5. Duration is long and cannot be shortened cheaply. Modified duration near 8.7 years with C$5,978m maturing in 2046 or later, including C$1,234m of 6.125% notes due 2115; low coupons lock in a long liability that cannot be captured on a rate decline without tender premiums.
  6. The pension surplus is non-cash income. C$415m of pre-tax recovery against C$13m of employer contributions, none of it distributable.
  7. Structural subordination is real and currently small, with the Mexican concession subsidiary and the KCS estate as non-guarantors.
  8. FX mismatch is the smallest. U.S. dollar debt is fully absorbed as a net investment hedge with no earnings effect, and a ten-cent currency move shifts leverage about 0.06x.
  9. The Mexican concession expires in 2047 with an asset-return obligation, and the longest-dated bond outlives it by 68 years.

Network fluidity is at a three-year best and still improving: Q2 2026 average train speed of 20.6 mph is the highest in the twelve-quarter window, terminal dwell of 8.6 hours the lowest, and locomotive productivity of 177 the highest since KCS was consolidated, achieved while train miles grew 3.6% against gross ton-mile growth of 5.5%, so it is not bought with extra train starts. Fuel efficiency inflected in the same quarter, the first sub-1.00 reading since Q1 2023 after three flat years, and still 19% behind CN. Headcount has come down and stayed down, with average employees 1.5% lower in Q2 2026 after a 0.9% decline in FY2025. Carload growth stopped: Q2 2026 carloads were flat and H1 carloads declined 1% while ton-miles rose, which is the length-of-haul extension arriving in the disclosed series. Fuel surcharge revenue rose 74% in one quarter on the diesel price and supplied 55% of the revenue increase. And both safety rates, which set 30% of the short-term incentive, deteriorated year over year in Q2 2026 after improving in FY2025. Two operating measures CPKC used to publish as levels — average train weight and average train length — have appeared only as percentage changes since the FY2021 10-K, while CN and UNP publish levels, so the cleanest cross-railroad measure of train-building discipline cannot be computed for CPKC from its SEC filings.

What drove the decade

Fuel is the swing item in both directions. Fuel expense moved from 8.5% of revenue in FY2020 to 15.9% in FY2022 and back to 11.5% in FY2025. It explains 5.2 points of the 2.3-point FY2022 operating-ratio deterioration and 0.9 points of the 1.6-point FY2025 improvement, partly offset inside the ratio because surcharge revenue is in the denominator.

Depreciation is the structural step-up. It rose from 9.7% of revenue in FY2022 to 13.4% in FY2025, the largest single change in the component table. C$376m of FY2025 depreciation and purchased services is amortization of KCS fair-value adjustments, worth 2.5 points of operating ratio, and it runs over the acquired assets' useful lives. That also distorts the reinvestment ratio: capex/depreciation of 1.56x in FY2025 appears to be a third below FY2019, but excluding the purchase-accounting charge the denominator is C$1,646m and the ratio is 1.91x, inside the FY2016–FY2021 range of 1.85x to 2.33x.

Labour intensity has declined steadily, from 21.8% of revenue in FY2016 to 17.1% in FY2025. Revenue per average employee rose from C$516k to C$755k and compensation per average employee from C$112k to C$129k.

FY2025 revenue growth was almost entirely volume. Ton-miles rose 3.8% while freight revenue per ton-mile was flat at 6.73 cents, which the 10-K composes as "higher freight rates and the favourable impact of the change in FX rates of $154 million, offset by the unfavourable impact of lower fuel prices on fuel surcharge revenues of $205 million."

Deleveraging came entirely from EBITDA. Net debt/EBITDA peaked at 4.99x at 2021 year end and was 3.02x at 2025 year end, while net debt went from C$20,058m to C$23,004m and total debt from C$20,127m to C$23,188m. Interest coverage stayed in a 6.4x to 9.1x band throughout the decade.

Two restatements break any spliced series. ASU 2017-07, adopted retrospectively on 2018-01-01, moved non-service pension components below operating income: FY2016 operating income restates from C$2,578m to C$2,411m and the operating ratio from 58.6% to 61.3%, so the best operating ratio the standalone CP network produced was 57.1% in FY2020 and not 57.4% in FY2017. And freight-car average in-service utilisation for 2022 was restated from 79% to 85% in the FY2023 10-K to harmonise methodology across the combined network, so pre-2023 operating statistics are CP-only.

14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

The headline disagreement is margin. Consensus requires about 145 basis points of operating-ratio improvement a year for three consecutive years. Management's own stated pace is 100 basis points a year, and the first half of 2026 delivered 70 basis points of deterioration. No North American Class I has improved its operating ratio for four consecutive years starting from a sub-65% base.▪

The estimates are Canadian dollars and CPKC's NYSE line is priced in U.S. dollars, so a P/E computed by dividing one by the other understates the multiple by the exchange rate: C$122.01 over C$5.171 is 23.6x, and Bloomberg's own field at the same override returns 23.595x. And the operating-income line blends two definitions, which is why the implied operating ratio cannot be set against either reported figure.

The near-term test is arithmetically specific. Consensus of C$5.171 for CY2026 requires second-half core adjusted EPS of C$2.871 against C$2.438 a year earlier, +17.8%, and second-half revenue of C$8,524m, +12.4%, after a first half that grew 5.5% and 5.0%.▪ Three things have to arrive together: volume accelerating from about 3% to about 7%; the fuel-surcharge lag turning from a third-quarter headwind into a fourth-quarter tailwind, which CPKC's treasurer supports by stating that 60% of the programme resets on a one-month lag against a two-month industry standard; and the share count falling under the 5% buyback. None of the three has a quantified contribution attached to it in any disclosure. Against them, management flags short-hauled plastics diverted to European markets in Q3 and a three-month IBEW strike that ran to 2026-08-24.

Dispersion is narrow where it is published and absent where it matters. Across 25 contributors, FY2026 revenue spans C$16.1bn to C$16.7bn, 3.7% of the mean, and EPS C$5.00 to C$5.37, 7.2%; the Bloomberg pull returns means only for CY2027 and CY2028, so the spread behind the out-year estimates is unmeasured. Two vendors also publish different FY2026 EPS for the same company on the same day — Bloomberg C$5.171 and MarketScreener C$4.863, a C$0.31 gap — which is the purchase-accounting wedge, running near C$0.40 for the full year on the disclosed H1 figures, and neither vendor labels its basis.

Six of the fourteen questions on the Q2 2026 call went to the UP–NS combination and the UP–CN side agreements. No consensus line contains a branch for denial, for approval with conditions, or for CPKC as a party to a subsequent transaction; the one quantified merger cost, C$27m of first-half advisory spend, is excluded from the core adjusted earnings the multiple is applied to. Four other drivers received no analyst question at all: the statutory revenue cap on about 7% of revenue and its 0.646% escalator for crop year 2026-27; the Mexican concession terms, rate registration and the 2026 tax reform requiring cash deposits to contest assessments; the recurring advisory cost itself; and pension income running C$71–111m above the level the 2024–2028 plan assumed, which is roughly C$0.08 a share after tax arising below the operating line.

Twelve of thirteen quarters landed within ±6% of consensus EPS and all thirteen within ±5% on revenue; seven beat and six missed. The reaction does not track the surprise. The two largest moves both followed EPS misses of under 2.5%, and the largest miss in the set moved the shares 0.3%. The mean EPS surprise is +0.2%, and the mean revenue surprise −0.4%, so CPKC lands almost exactly on the consensus earnings number while running slightly below the consensus revenue number, with cost and below-the-line items making up the difference. What reconciles a two-point average annual guidance shortfall with a roughly zero quarterly surprise is the mid-year guidance cut: the street marks down to the revised guide and CPKC then hits the marked-down number. Q4 2025 broke that pattern, missing both the reaffirmed annual guide and the quarterly consensus.

Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
Q1 2024 −6.3% Core adjusted combined EPS of C$0.93 grew 3% against a full-year double-digit guide and the core adjusted operating ratio was 50bp worse, with operating income flat on 2% revenue growth. Volume guidance was held at low single digits and the CEO called it "responsibly conservative" against an unresolved Teamsters negotiation with a 19 May drop-dead date; asked whether double-digit EPS survived a strike he would commit only to "if we have kind of a strike that's not extended". The shares went into the print at C$119.77, near the then-record C$123.13
Q4 2025 +5.4% The print missed slightly on both lines; the 2026 package did not. Mid-single-digit ton-mile growth plus low double-digit earnings growth explicitly without macro help, a record Canadian grain harvest of 85 million tonnes against a previous record of 78 million moving through 2026, a new 5% repurchase programme, and capex cut 15% to C$2.65bn. Full-year core adjusted operating ratio improved 140bp to 59.9%
Q2 2026 −3.9% A low-quality beat into a share price that had run to C$128.36. Of the C$465m revenue increase C$258m was fuel surcharge, cents per ton-mile rose 9% "reflecting higher fuel surcharge revenue", and fuel expense rose 53%. Coal revenue declined 18% on a 29% volume decline and management guided coal to remain a headwind in the second half. The CMO named refined fuels into Mexico as "the one area that keeps me up at night… pretty well nonexistent here for the last 6, 8 months"
Q1 2026 +2.5% A 2.4% EPS miss framed as planned seasonality and offset by a reaffirmation: "I fully expect us to return to double-digit EPS growth here in Q2 and the second half." Q1 grain set records, management said April would be "a record month for us across the board in CPKC history", and C$680m of buybacks lifted shareholder-return spend 69%

The deepest, −38.2% from March 2015 to January 2016, ran through a revenue contraction from C$6,712m in 2015 to C$6,232m in 2016 and the January 2016 commodity selloff, with the largest single-day declines on 2016-01-06 (−6.5%) and 2016-01-13 (−5.2%). The trough date is the Q4 2015 earnings date itself, and the shares rose 10.6% the following session. Over the same months CP pursued Norfolk Southern and terminated on 2016-04-11; Pershing Square sold its entire remaining holding in Q3 2016, and Hunter Harrison retired with Creel appointed CEO effective 2017-01-31.

The 2021 decline of 16.8% is the KCS contest priced in real time: −5.4% on the session after the original agreement was announced, −5.7% during the competing-bid period on 2021-07-08, and the STB's rejection of CN's voting trust straddling −4.6% on 2021-08-31 and +5.1% the next day. The trough came a week after KCS accepted the raised offer, and the position was not recovered until 2022-03-07. The price agreed is visible on the balance sheet: shares outstanding went from 666.5m at 2020 year end to 929.7m a year later and common equity from C$7,319m to C$33,829m.

The longest, −22.3% over thirteen months from the March 2024 record, has three dated legs: the Q1 2024 print taking 6.3% off in a session; −5.7% on 2025-02-03 as tariffs on Canada and Mexico were announced and then paused; and a trough on 2025-04-08, the third session after the 2025-04-02 U.S. tariff announcement, followed by +7.9% on 2025-04-09 when the pause was announced. A further leg followed the proposed UP–NS combination, with −3.6% on 2025-07-18. One secondary account attributes the April 2025 low to CPKC's guidance cut and reports a 5.8% single-day decline (co24.ca, accessed 2026-09-21) [web, unverified]; the Bloomberg daily series does not support it, showing +0.5% on 2025-04-30 and +0.5% on 2025-05-01, and places the drawdown low three weeks before the cut on tariff news.

Every forward year was revised down over the past twelve months — CY2026 by 4.3%, CY2027 by 1.7%, CY2028 by 1.8% — while the shares rose 16.8% in Canadian dollars. Estimates then stabilised: CY2026 bottomed at C$5.042 on 2026-07-03, three weeks before the Q2 print, and has recovered 2.6%. Against four listed comparables on the same snapshot, CPKC has the smallest three-month upward revision and the second-largest twelve-month cut: CP +0.9% and −4.3%, CN +3.8% and −2.1%, UNP +3.8% and +1.8%, CSX +4.8% and +4.1%, NSC +6.3% and −7.7%.

Between 2025-12-31 and 2026-09-21 the shares rose 20.7% in Canadian dollars. Over the same period the 12-month-forward consensus EPS rose 8.2%, from C$5.320 to C$5.757, and the 12-month-forward multiple rose 11.6%, from 19.0x to 21.2x, while the full-year CY2026 estimate moved the other way from C$5.320 to C$5.171. Most of the year's price gain is a change in what the market pays per dollar of expected earnings.

17. Forward model summary

Year zero is FY2025 as filed: revenue C$15,078m, operating expense C$9,469m, operating income C$5,609m, core adjusted operating ratio 59.9%, core adjusted diluted EPS C$4.61, 219,420m revenue ton-miles, 403,891m gross ton-miles, 4,514.0 thousand carloads, net debt C$23,004m and 917.1m diluted shares. Because CPKC reports one segment and allocates no cost to any commodity line, revenue is built nine ways and cost once at the company level, and no line-level margin appears in the output. Four identities hold in every year: the nine lines plus fuel surcharge plus non-freight equal total revenue; gross ton-miles are ton-miles times the disclosed 1.8408 ratio, which was 1.840 in FY2024; fuel expense is gross ton-miles times efficiency times the diesel price times the exchange rate, which reproduces FY2025 at C$1,732m against C$1,731m reported; and net debt moves by dividends plus repurchases less free cash flow.

Revenue is built from ton-miles and yield per ton-mile by line, with the fuel surcharge modelled separately because CPKC discloses it only in total and it moves revenue and expense by almost the same amount. Cost is built from gross ton-miles and headcount. Below the operating line are interest on average debt, the pension recovery and a flat tax rate.

Revenue compounds at 3.8% a year over seven years and core adjusted EPS at 6.7%.

FY2026 revenue growth is mostly diesel. The change from FY2025 is volume and mix +C$500m, base yield −C$50m, fuel surcharge +C$567m and non-freight +C$8m. The surcharge supplies 55% of the increase, the same share it supplied in Q2 2026, and base freight revenue excluding it grows 3.4%.

FY2027 is the crop year. Revenue grows 1.1% and core adjusted EPS 3.4%, because grain ton-miles decline while the diesel assumption steps down, taking C$160m out of surcharge revenue. Coal recovering offsets about half the grain reversion in ton-miles and less in revenue, because coal is the lowest-yield line at 4.31 cents against grain's 5.24.

The reported and underlying margins move in opposite directions in 2026. Core adjusted operating ratio goes from 59.9% to 61.1%, 120bp worse, while the ratio computed with surcharge revenue and fuel expense removed from both sides improves from 56.9% to 56.7%. Surcharge is recognised at a 100% incremental operating ratio, so C$567m of extra surcharge with matching fuel expense on a C$15bn base dilutes the reported ratio by roughly 140bp on its own. Over the full seven years the ex-surcharge ratio improves 160bp, 23bp a year, against management's stated 100bp a year.

Cumulative FY2026–FY2032: operating cash flow C$43,256m, capex C$20,015m, free cash flow C$23,241m, dividends C$7,389m and repurchases C$21,376m. Shareholder returns of C$28,765m are 1.24x cumulative free cash flow, net debt rises C$5,523m, and net debt/EBITDA never reaches the stated 2.75x target inside the forecast.

The bull's 52.1% core adjusted operating ratio in FY2032, and 54.6% by FY2030, would put CPKC outside the recorded range of the entire Class I class from 2030: the lowest full year any member has reported since 1995 is CSX's 55.3% in 2021, and CPKC's own best is 59.9% core adjusted and 57.1% on the legacy Canada-only network at recession volumes, on a company where 18% of revenue is generated on a Mexican concession whose closest listed comparison ran a 72.5% operating ratio in FY2025. The bear's 68.4% is worse than CPKC has ever printed, between CSX's FY2025 67.9% and Grupo México Transportes' 72.5%. Even the bull reaches management's 2028 doubling late: it delivers C$6.69 in FY2028 and crosses C$7.68 in FY2030.

Volume dominates because only about 40–55% of an average cost dollar recurs on the next ton-mile, so incremental ton-miles arrive at high margin in both directions: a 1.5-point move is worth C$2,104m of the FY2032 operating-income range. Base yield is second at C$1,557m for one point, because an additional cent of rate on an already-scheduled train consumes almost no cost. Capital intensity is the largest cash-only driver, moving free cash flow C$839m across a 14.5%-to-18.0% span with no operating-income effect for several years. Headcount elasticity and wage growth do less: the whole 0.35-to-0.60 span of headcount elasticity moves FY2032 operating income C$101m, about 1.3%, and compensation per employee across 2.7% to 3.4% moves it C$139m. Together they are worth less than a quarter of what 1.5 points of volume is worth.
