Six of these assumptions are weaker than the table implies, and two are contradicted by evidence dated September 2026.

The diesel price is wrong in the direction that matters least for earnings and most for the reported ratio. U.S. retail on-highway diesel reached US$6.285 on 2026-09-14 after US$5.257 on 2026-08-10, US$2.546 above a year earlier (eia.gov, accessed 2026-09-21) [web]. CPKC's own price has run near 0.81x that index, which puts a full year closer to US$4.25 than the US$3.94 assumed [estimate: Q3 retail near US$5.6 and Q4 near US$6.3 at 0.81x; range US$4.1–4.5]. The consequence is roughly C$160m more FY2026 surcharge revenue with matching fuel expense and about 40bp more reported operating-ratio dilution, and almost nothing at the operating line.

The repurchase price cannot be flat. Every disclosed CPKC programme executed at a rising price: C$107.61 across 37.3m shares in 2025 and C$117.18 across 16.6m in H1 2026, 8.9% higher in six months, and the CFO described the 2014–2020 programme as buying "at half the price of what we're trading today". Holding C$117.18 for seven years while the same model compounds earnings 6.7% a year buys at a falling multiple. C$21,376m of repurchases at C$117.18 retires 182m shares; at a price escalating with earnings it retires about 147m, which would make FY2032 core adjusted EPS roughly C$6.90 instead of C$7.24 [estimate: average price near C$145 across 2026–2032 at the model's own earnings growth rate; range C$0.25–0.40 of FY2032 EPS]. The 2% Canadian repurchase tax, C$77m in 2025 and C$36m in H1 2026, adds a further 2% to the effective cost and is not in the price.

The FY2027 grain assumption has been overtaken by a measurement. The base case reverts the crop toward its five-year mean by arithmetic. Statistics Canada's September 2026 estimate puts prairie wheat at 36.1 Mt, 10.9% below 2025 and still above the 33.4 Mt five-year average, and canola at 22.1 Mt, 0.8% below, on record acreage (Statistics Canada production estimate published 2026-09-16, www150.statcan.gc.ca, accessed 2026-09-21) [web]. Seven of FY2027's twelve months ship that crop, so only five months are exposed to a reversion, and weighting those months gives about −4% for the line against the −7% assumed and the −14% bear.

The company-weighted base yield of 1.75% a year from FY2029 is the second-largest driver in the model and the least supported. Two observations exist on the merged network, +0.7% in FY2025 and +0.4% in H1 2026 after stripping surcharge and the disclosed FX effect, and the base assumes three to four times the more recent one. The stated mechanism is that length-of-haul dilution exhausts, and length of haul grew 3.7% in H1 2026 against 0.5% in FY2025, so the dilution accelerated at the last observation. Management's own renewal claim was described two ways four weeks apart: "exceeding the top end of our 3% to 4% outlook" on the Q1 2026 call and "around 3.5% pricing recently" at BofA on 2026-05-13. One point of company base yield is C$1,557m of the FY2032 operating-income range, and the bear's 0.75% is the realized rate continued.

Four line-level volume rates run above their own seasonal run-rates. Energy, chemicals and plastics grew 0.2% in H1 2026 and the line's 2024–2025 average second-half-to-first-half ratio implies about +0.6% for the second half, while the base requires +5.0%. Potash needs +6.0% in the second half against a run-rate of −0.6%, with port maintenance and lower mine production continuing and Canpotex committed only through the first half. Fertilizers and sulphur needs +3.9% against a run-rate of −3.2%, on a line whose carloads were flat in both recent periods. Intermodal needs +7.0% against a seasonal +3.4%. Grain, metals and minerals, automotive and forest products each reconcile to their run-rates within about 1.5 points. On the coal line the base needs a second half at −11.9% against a run-rate of −17.1% and an H1 of −19.7%, which requires lifting quarterly ton-miles about 21% above the Q2 level in a half management guides as a headwind; the bear's −22.0% is the more defensible figure and Glencore's reaffirmed 30–32 Mt guidance is why it is not refuted outright.

Three cost elasticities do not reproduce either disclosed period. The materials formula gives 5.7% growth for FY2025 against an actual of 16.7% and 5.8% for H1 2026 against 3.6%. Equipment rents gives 4.9% against +17.6% and −5.0%. Purchased services gives 4.1% against −4.0% and +0.4%, on a C$2,256m line, which biases the modelled cost line high by roughly C$185m a year on the FY2025-sized gap and therefore understates operating income. Track material consumption follows the rail and crosstie programme, 285 track miles and 1,652 thousand crossties in FY2025, which is a capital-plan decision and not a function of gross ton-miles, and 15,093 of 51,971 freight cars are leased, so equipment rents steps with lease renewals.

The depreciation and capital assumptions are not consistent with each other. Non-KCS depreciation is driven off revenue growth in a year when 55% of the revenue increase is diesel pass-through, so roughly C$30m of FY2026 depreciation is generated by a surcharge that supports no asset. At the other end, cumulative capex of C$20,015m against cumulative depreciation of C$15,425m takes capex to 1.29x depreciation by FY2032, below CPKC's ten-year range of 1.51x to 2.33x. The capital ratio itself is also at or below the decade floor: 16.0% of revenue against a ten-year range of 17.7% to 21.7%, although on revenue excluding the surcharge the base is about 18.5%, inside the record, and management has stated C$2.6–2.8bn a year as sustainable.

Three financing assumptions are held as single points across all three scenarios. The tax rate is right for 2026 and flat to FY2032 against a ten-year realized range of 22.24% to 26.42%, a 4.2-point band worth about C$0.25 of FY2032 EPS at the extremes, with Mexican tax reform effective 2026-01-01 and a 2014 assessment in litigation neither sized. The exchange rate of 1.38 is below the 1.4035 spot on 2026-09-21 and below the FY2025 average of 1.3975, and each C$0.01 moves revenue about C$78m and operating income about C$33m. Stock-based compensation is held at C$60m a year against a ten-year range of C$35m to C$170m and a sensitivity that doubled inside 2026 to C$2.2–2.4m per C$1.00 of share price, so a C$20 move swings the line about C$45m. The bull, at 14.0% earnings growth, is the scenario that would pay it.

The leverage constraint does not bind. Repurchases stop at 3.60x net debt/EBITDA and resume below 3.10x, against management's stated 2.75x. The base path peaks at 3.27x and never reaches 2.75x, so the constraint is inactive in the base and the bull, and the repurchase assumption is unconstrained; S&P holds a positive outlook on BBB+ while the same ratio rises.

Seven assumptions hold on their own evidence: the FY2026 headcount average of 19,900, which implies a second half consistent with the assumed volume; the 0.45 headcount elasticity, against negative realized readings in both merged-network observations; the 0.5% a year fuel-efficiency gain, a sixth of the realized H1 2026 rate; the C$373m KCS amortization, confirmed in two independent periods; the 3.86% effective interest rate, which two independent computations agree on; the C$0.98 2026 dividend, three-quarters of which is already declared; and the 1.4m of annual option issuance, against a draining pool of about 5.3m options.

Checks against the company's own record

Ex-fuel incremental margins in the base case are 48% in FY2026, 26% in the crop-reversion year and 49–54% from FY2028, against CPKC's realized 51%, 59% and 57% in FY2017–FY2019, negative in FY2021 and FY2022, 30% in FY2023, 45% in FY2024 and 75% in FY2025, with organic figures of 68% in FY2025 and 40% in H1 2026. The base is at the median of that record and below management's guided 60–70%, and no base-case year exceeds the company's best. Three bull years do. The base's FY2032 core adjusted operating ratio of 59.3% is 60bp better than FY2025 and inside everything CPKC has printed. Against the Class I reference class, the base's three-year revenue CAGR of 3.7% is roughly the 58th percentile of windows beginning at or above a prior revenue peak, where the class median is 2.4%, and its three-year EPS CAGR of 5.5% is roughly the 38th percentile conditional on a sub-65% operating-ratio start, where the class median is 9.0%. The base is above the class median on revenue and below it on earnings, and the reason is margin: every window in the class that beat 14% a year on earnings also delivered a large operating-ratio improvement.

The UP–NS outcome enters the model only as an advisory cost, because CPKC does not disaggregate interline or gateway revenue and the exposure cannot be sized from the filings, while the statutory decision deadline of 2027-08-28 falls inside the forecast. No scenario models a Mexican concession or rate-regulation event; the bear reduces Mexican-exposed volume growth instead.

18. Risks

Ranking is by disclosed revenue, earnings or balance-sheet value at stake over three years, weighted by how far each mechanism has already advanced.

1. The UP–NS decision resets CPKC's gateway and interline economics, and the exposure cannot be sized. Traffic CPKC hands to UP or NS at Chicago, Kansas City, Memphis or New Orleans becomes traffic a merged carrier can route end to end, and the pricing tension between two connections at a gateway collapses to one.▪ Creel put the merged carrier at "40% of every move" across 43 states and said approval means "it's a matter of time, there's going to be additional consolidation. There has to be." CN has already signed with UP. No CPKC filing gives interline revenue, revenue by gateway or revenue divisions with connecting carriers, so the exposure cannot be sized from the disclosure and the only measured number is the cost of fighting: C$27m in H1 2026, C$21m after tax, two cents of diluted EPS. Leading indicators: the conditions CPKC requests on 2026-11-18, the quarterly advisory-cost line, the replies due 2027-02-16, and the decision due by 2027-08-28.

2. Mexico: concession, tax assessment and peso. CPKCM operates on a concession to June 2047 and does not own the land, roadway or structures; exclusive freight rights extend only to 2037; it pays 1.25% of gross revenues annually, registers maximum rates with ATTRAPI, and must meet investment commitments in a three-year plan filed with SICT. On termination or revocation "CPKCM would receive no compensation and its interest in its rail lines… would revert to the Mexican government." Exposure: C$2,711m of FY2025 revenue, 18.0%, and C$11,326m of properties and right-of-use assets, 20.3% of the total.▪ The 2014 SAT assessment stood at Ps.6,667m (C$540m) at 2026-06-30 including inflation, interest and penalties, and grows each period; Mexican tax reform effective 2026-01-01 requires a cash deposit to contest an assessment. An injunction against enforcement was granted 2025-08-20 while the assessment is guaranteed, and CPKC registered a CPTPP arbitration against Mexico at ICSID on 2026-04-27, after four years of domestic process. Leading indicators: the Circuit Court ruling on the second Amparo appeal, migration of further assessments from administrative appeal into litigation, ATTRAPI rate registrations, and a Comisión Nacional Antimonopolios finding of no effective competition.

3. Origin-counterparty concentration on 11% of revenue, already realised. Canadian coal "originates mainly from Elk Valley Resources' mines", all export potash is marketed by Canpotex or K+S, and the two lines are C$1,665m of FY2025 revenue. Q2 2026 coal revenue declined to C$209m from C$256m on carloads down 20% and ton-miles down 29%, and Glencore's own report confirms Canadian production down 19% in the half with full-year guidance cut. Coal alone costs about two points of group volume growth in 2026. Leading indicators: Glencore's quarterly Elk Valley production, British Columbia and federal permitting decisions in the Elk Valley, and Canpotex committed-volume commentary in CPKC's quarterly remarks.

4. Statutory revenue cap on the largest line. The maximum revenue entitlement caps aggregate revenue on western Canadian export grain to Vancouver and Thunder Bay by a formula on volume, length of haul, average revenue per ton and an inflation index. Grain was 21.3% of FY2025 revenue and the regulated portion C$1,067m in crop year 2024-25, 33% of the line and 7.1% of total revenue. CPKC is not approaching the cap; it exceeded it by C$2,660,250 and paid a 5% penalty. The escalator for crop year 2026-27 is +0.646%, near the bottom of a disclosed series that has ranged from −3% to +12.7%, and H1 2026 grain revenue ran 17% higher on ton-miles up 16%. Leading indicators: the Agency's annual index determination, any Canada Transportation Act review or interswitching amendment, and CPKC's disclosed grain revenue per ton-mile.

5. The second half of 2026 has to deliver a step-up no disclosed series yet supports. H1 2026 core adjusted EPS grew 5.5%. The low end of "low double-digit" implies C$5.07 and a second half of C$2.77, +14%; consensus of C$5.171 implies C$2.87 and +18%. Creel reaffirmed on 2026-09-17 with ton-miles "about 4% year to date" and "knocking on 7%" quarter to date, coal costing about two points, a Q3 fuel-surcharge lag correcting in Q4, and a three-month IBEW strike behind. CPKC's initial annual earnings guide was met twice in six closed years, and in 2025 the cut guide was also missed. Leading indicators: Q3 2026 core adjusted EPS, weekly ton-miles, and the surcharge line against On-Highway Diesel.

6. Operating ratio deterioration and casualty cost. Core adjusted operating ratio worsened year over year in both 2026 quarters, 50bp in Q1 and 90bp in Q2, after improving 140bp in FY2025. Two drivers are disclosed. The Q2 and first-half MD&A each name "an increase in casualty incident costs" as the leading driver of higher purchased services and other, and the CFO sized casualty, stock-based and incentive compensation together at about C$0.05 of EPS and close to 150 basis points, against C$0.04 and 120bp in the same call's prepared remarks. The second is the surcharge, entering at a 100% operating ratio. Against that, the FY2025 10-K reports both FRA frequency rates improving, so frequency and casualty expense moved in opposite directions. Leading indicators: the purchased services line and its stated drivers each quarter, and the quarterly FRA rates, which deteriorated year to date in 2026.

7. Hazardous-materials catastrophe with insurance exhaustion. As a common carrier CPKC must move crude oil, ethanol and toxic-inhalation materials including chlorine and anhydrous ammonia "regardless of risk or potential exposure to loss", and the risk factor states claims "could exceed the existing insurance coverage commercially available to the Company." CPKC does not publish a per-occurrence limit, retention or premium. The peer number sizes it: Norfolk Southern's Eastern Ohio derailment produced approximately US$1.1bn of recognised insurance recoveries across 2023–2025 and its FY2025 10-K states "In 2025, we exhausted coverage under our liability insurance policies with respect to the Incident", with US$191m of incident-related environmental liabilities still outstanding. One derailment consumed an entire liability tower. CPKC's own long-tail litigation has resolved in its favour: every Lac-Mégantic claim was dismissed, upheld on appeal, and the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed all three leave applications on 2026-05-14, and the Maine bankruptcy-estate claim was dismissed on summary judgement on 2026-04-21 with no appeal. Remaining live items are the Remington Development claim, returned to first instance after the Alberta Court of Appeal ordered a new trial and the Supreme Court dismissed leave on 2026-07-02; environmental remediation provisions of C$248m at 2026-06-30 payable through 2035; and an EPA Clean Air Act enquiry into locomotive compliance open since September 2020 with a draft consent decree since December 2022. Leading indicators: quarterly casualty commentary, the environmental provision balance, and the FRA train accident rate.

8. Labour, where binding arbitration has become the default. Nearly 75% of the workforce is unionised across 73 units: eight Canadian units covering about 7,000 employees, 63 U.S. units covering about 4,300 under the Railway Labor Act, and about 3,300 in Mexico. The Teamsters Canada Rail Conference agreements came out of binding arbitration on 2025-05-30 at 3% a year to 2027-12-31. About 300 IBEW signals and communications employees struck from 2026-05-31 until the parties agreed to binding arbitration on 2026-08-21 and returned 2026-08-24, roughly twelve weeks of disrupted signals maintenance inside Q2 and Q3 2026 (newswire.ca, accessed 2026-09-21) [web]. CPKC does not disclose the strike's revenue or cost effect. One Canadian agreement runs to 2026-12-31, two to 2027-12-31, three to 2028-12-31 and one to 2029-12-31; in the U.S. 19 of 63 units had tentative agreements with 16 ratified. Leading indicators: where the arbitrated IBEW award lands against the 3% pattern, the December 2026 Canadian renewal, and Canadian labour-reform legislation tabled the week of 2026-09-14.

9. Trade policy. Cross-border traffic between the three countries is the merger thesis and is 41% of FY2025 freight revenue.▪ Realised effects are already in the lines: Q4 2025 forest products revenue declined 13% on volumes down 12% attributed to Canadian lumber tariffs and H1 2026 forest products declined 8%; cross-border steel is "still effectively shut off"; automotive took a C$30m revenue headwind in Q4 2025 from production slowdowns and component supply; Mexican refined fuels have "been pretty well nonexistent here for the last 6, 8 months". The United States declined to extend USMCA at the 2026-07-01 joint review, converting it into an annual process to 2036, and imposed 50% duties on a range of Canadian goods from 2026-08-19, which land entirely in Q3 2026. Leading indicators: annual review milestones, forest-products and metals volumes, and whether the Mexican refined-fuel arbitrage reopens.

10. Fuel surcharge as a margin and revenue distortion. About 10% of FY2025 freight revenue, indexed to On-Highway Diesel and PEMEX TAR Irapuato, entering at a 100% operating ratio, with roughly 60% of the programme on a one-month lag and the remainder on two months. A diesel spike lifts revenue and worsens the reported ratio at the same time, and CPKC books the cost before the recovery. The Canadian federal carbon tax ended 2025-04-01, permanently removing the carbon-levy component. Leading indicator: the disclosed quarterly surcharge line against On-Highway Diesel.

11. Buybacks funded with debt. Total debt went from C$23,188m at 2025-12-31 to C$25,147m at 2026-06-30, up C$1,959m in six months, against C$1,963m of repurchases. H1 2026 operating cash flow less capital additions left C$1,267m against C$2,371m of returns, funded with C$1,621m of new notes at 4.00% and 5.50% and C$284m of net commercial paper. Retained earnings declined from C$19,783m to C$19,727m despite C$1,870m of net income. Part of the debt increase is translation of U.S.-dollar and peso debt. Leading indicators: the quarterly buyback table against free cash flow, commercial paper outstanding, and the rating agencies' outlooks, which are currently positive at S&P and stable at Moody's.

12. Interline disputes with a merger applicant. CPKC dispatches the Meridian Speedway, a joint venture in which Norfolk Southern holds an interest. On the Q3 2025 call Creel described restricting NS to 8,500-foot trains because the line was built for that length, NS objecting, CPKC preparing an STB filing, and NS paying CPKC for delays under a temporary arrangement pending a second train start: "I'm not going to subsidize NS' operation nor am I going to subsidize UP's operation for their operational synergies at the cost of my service to my customers." The counterparty is one of the two merger applicants and the STB is the forum for both matters. CPKC reports Meridian Speedway additions separately at C$13m in H1 2026, which sizes the capital commitment and not the traffic. Leading indicator: STB docket filings on the Speedway.

13. Climate physical risk. The FY2025 factor was expanded and its language hardened from conditional to realised: impacts "have necessitated and in the future could necessitate significant capital investments to enhance infrastructure resilience", with wildfires, drought and regional water stress added as named hazards, and insurance that "may not continue to be available at commercially reasonable rates." The exposed segment is the Canadian mountain corridor between the Elk Valley, the Prairies and Vancouver, and Q2 2026 coal volumes already suffered from port maintenance at Vancouver, Kamloops and Thunder Bay.

14. KCS integration has not finished being a cost. The STB's seven-year oversight period from the 2023-03-15 decision runs to 2030, with conditions on keeping gateways open on commercially reasonable terms, creating no new bottlenecks, and data reporting. Purchase-accounting amortization was C$187m in H1 2026 and cost 2.4 points of operating ratio, with another C$36m of acquisition-related costs, and the FY2025 10-K states CPKC "continues to expect to incur acquisition-related costs beyond the year of acquisition".

Which risks arrive together: A poor western Canadian harvest with an Elk Valley shortfall and a port maintenance window hits grain and coal at once, 28% of revenue in unit-train bulk at two of the three lowest yields, so ton-miles decline faster than revenue against a cost base that does not flex. A diesel spike, a derailment and a rising share price raise surcharge dilution, casualty expense and cash-settled compensation together, which is what cost about 150 basis points in Q2 2026. Tariff escalation in an annual USMCA review suppresses cross-border automotive, steel and refined-fuel flows while a peso move cuts translated Mexican revenue and a tax enforcement step forces a cash deposit. And STB approval of UP–NS would, on Creel's own view, trigger further consolidation, putting a competitive step-change and the cost of CPKC's own response together at a point when debt has already risen C$1,959m in six months to fund repurchases.

19. Source disclosure

Company filings and transcripts: Ten annual reports on Form 10-K covering FY2016 to FY2025 and six quarterly reports through 2026-Q2, with cleaned text; 24 earnings-call transcripts from Q3 2020 to Q2 2026, contiguous; 76 presentation transcripts from 2016-11-30 to 2026-09-17, including the 2018 and 2023 Analyst and Investor Days, four 2021 KCS merger calls, ten annual shareholder calls and the March 2020 special call; eleven investor decks from October 2014 to September 2026 with 523 rendered slides; 24 earnings releases furnished on Form 8-K; the 2026 management information circular filed 2026-03-25 and the FY2022 through FY2025 Form 10-K/A Part III amendments; and SEC XBRL company facts for CIK 0000016875 covering FY2008 to FY2025.

Peer and counterparty filings: FY2025 10-Ks and 2026 Q1 and Q2 10-Qs for Union Pacific, Norfolk Southern, CSX, BNSF, Wabtec and Mosaic; Canadian National's FY2025 40-F and 2026 Q1 and Q2 6-K exhibits; Nutrien's FY2025 40-F management discussion and financial statements; and SEC company-concept data for Kansas City Southern through FY2022.

Market data: Bloomberg terminal, pulled fresh on 2026-09-21: daily prices and total-return indices for both CPKC listings from 2014, the monthly forward-expectations history from 2014, current estimates by fiscal year through CY2029, annual reported fundamentals, thirteen quarters of actual-versus-estimate pairs with next-session reactions, and the comparable-company table. Annual Bloomberg fundamentals for eight North American Class I railroads from FY1995 to FY2025, 289 company-years, supplied the base-rate distributions in Section 14.

Data built from those sources: A 1,521-row annual and 1,094-row quarterly financial series reconciled across three sources; a nine-line commodity revenue, volume and yield series; an 80-assumption driver model with three scenarios and 1,655 rows of projections; a 33-column comparable table; and four price and multiple charts.

Gaps and failures: No sell-side research on CPKC is available, so the external view in Section 14 is built from Bloomberg consensus and named web sources. CPKC's executive compensation is not on EDGAR as a DEF 14A — the last was filed 2017-03-16 and the company is exempt from SEC proxy rules as a Canadian MJDS issuer — so Section 10 uses the circular furnished as an 8-K exhibit and the Part III amendments; pay-mix and peer-group drift are described from the 2026 circular's own retrospective. Canadian-market insider transactions file to SEDI and not to EDGAR, so the Form 144 record is the U.S. leg only. CPKC's own "Core adjusted ROIC" and "Adjusted free cash" reconciliations for FY2024 and FY2025 are in quarterly supplemental data files on the company's investor site that are not in the archive, so both measures appear here as explicit reconstructions. Fuel surcharge revenue levels for FY2016 and FY2017 are not stated in any archived filing, so ex-surcharge growth begins at FY2019. Item 5 share-price high-low tables end with the FY2017 10-K, so buyback timing is tested against CPKC's own monthly average prices paid. The revolving credit agreement's financial covenant and its level do not appear in any 10-K since at least FY2020. The Canadian Transportation Agency's 2026-27 index determination was reachable only through a secondary report that returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch. Grain's Canada-versus-U.S. and coal's metallurgical-thermal-petroleum-coke splits appear in Item 1 only as pie-chart images; the investor deck supplies them and is cited where used. Grupo México Transportes returns no current Bloomberg price, so the only Mexican rail comparable is blank throughout Section 16, and Berkshire's price-to-book did not return on two field attempts.

Discrepancies left unresolved: The FY2025 10-K states the after-tax gain on the Panama Canal Railway sale as US$177m (C$256m) and the Q2 2026 10-Q states US$196m (C$282m) for the same transaction, with the pre-tax US$232m (C$333m) agreed in both; the FY2025 significant-items note reconciles the difference as C$26m of additional current tax recorded later in 2025, so the 10-Q quotes the quarter and the 10-K the year. Bloomberg records FY2022 revenue of C$13,217m and diluted EPS of C$4.45 against the filed C$8,814m and C$3.77, because Bloomberg applies a KCS-combined restatement to 2022 but not to 2021; the filed figures are used. The FY2022 10-K reports a 2022 adjusted operating ratio of 61.4% while the FY2023 and FY2024 10-Ks report 61.7% for the same year on a combined basis that gives effect to KCS from 2022-01-01; both are labelled and answer different questions. Two figures exist for the Q2 2026 casualty and compensation headwind, C$0.04 and 120bp in prepared remarks against C$0.05 and about 150bp in the Q&A of the same call. Published September 2026 coking coal prices disagree across publishers by up to US$60 per tonne, so Glencore's own realised price is used. A third-party rendering of the Q2 2026 call prints an operating ratio of 54.6% and core adjusted EPS of C$1.20 against the 10-Q's 64.6% and C$1.27; the filing is used.

Web sources: Thirty-six distinct pages across 35 domains support the claims tagged [web], with the passage for each quoted in Appendix B. Only one domain is used more than once: stb.gov (2). Two claims are tagged [web, unverified] because the page could not be re-fetched or the series does not support it: the Canadian Transportation Agency's 2026-27 index determination, reported by railwayage.com, which returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch, and the co24.ca account of the April 2025 guidance cut, which the Bloomberg daily series contradicts.

Estimates: Twenty-one figures above are tagged [estimate:] and each states its method and range. By method: five use car tare and lading physics scaled to the disclosed system gross-ton-mile total (the unit-economics cost column and everything derived from it, including the per-gross-ton-mile yield spread); four apply the September 2026 deck's commodity sub-split percentages to disclosed freight revenue (regulated grain, Mexico-origin vehicles, cross-border intermodal, land-bridge weight); three derive tonnes or units per railcar from disclosed ton-miles and carloads over an assumed haul distance (the freight-as-a-share-of-value table); two reconstruct a withdrawn non-GAAP measure from disclosed inputs (core adjusted return on invested capital and adjusted free cash conversion); two build an enterprise value or net debt from a disclosed price, share count and leverage ratio (the KCS deal multiples); and two project a forward path from a disclosed run-rate (the refinancing cost and the FY2026 diesel price). No estimate is presented as a point figure without its range where the underlying inputs are bounded.

20. What we still don't know, and the metrics that would resolve it

Named gaps that remain open:

  • Mexican profitability. Mexico produced 18% of FY2025 revenue and holds roughly 20% of net property, and no profit, margin or return figure for it exists in any CPKC disclosure. The Section 3 assessment of the concession's contribution and the Section 11 judgment on the KCS price both stand without knowing whether the largest block of capital earns above the industry cost of capital. Two routes would resolve it: the STB Annual Report Form R-1 filed by Soo Line Railroad Company and The Kansas City Southern Railway Company, which is the only public source for a U.S.-only income statement and investment base at a one-segment reporter, and Kansas City Southern's own FY2016–FY2021 disclosures split between its U.S. and Mexican reportable segments while it was a separate registrant.
  • Mexican concession renewal. The concession runs to June 2047 with exclusive freight rights only to 2037, and C$9,176m of concession rights inside the purchase price allocation is amortized over a 74-year assumption that extends ten years past the exclusivity. The renewal terms, the price and what happens to the exclusive right in 2037 are the largest unexamined accounting judgment on the balance sheet.
  • Metals, minerals and consumer products. The line is 11.9% of revenue and supplied 19.4% of H1 2026 revenue growth, and it has three unrelated exposures named: frac-sand completions, cement and aggregate construction, and cross-border steel at a 50% tariff. The 3.5% a year rate that feeds the base case has no decomposition behind it.
  • The two halves of intermodal. The disclosed 54% domestic and 46% international split is never forecast separately in any published line, and the model holds international flat by assumption. The fastest-growing line in the base case blends a leg CPKC sells directly with a leg four ocean alliances allocate annually.
  • Canadian shipper remedies. Whether the 160-km extended interswitching regime remains in force in 2026, and how much CPKC-origin traffic falls inside a competing carrier's reach under it, long-haul interswitching, final-offer arbitration and level-of-service complaints. This is the third term in the regulatory assessment and it is unsized.
  • Interline and gateway revenue. Ten years of 10-Ks disaggregate revenue by commodity and by country and never by connection or gateway, which is why the UP–NS exposure cannot be sized. The STB's own docket record, including the applicants' revised application of 2026-04-30 and its traffic diversion studies, is public and would constrain it.
  • Land-bridge revenue against an audited series. The C$100m-to-C$600m-to-C$1bn path exists only in management commentary. The STB Carload Waybill Sample, which reports origin-destination revenue per ton-mile by lane, is the nearest independent check.
  • Intra-quarter and weekly operating data. CPKC-specific AAR weekly carloads by commodity group and the STB's weekly Rail Service Data on velocity, dwell and cars online would independently test the second-half acceleration that Sections 14 and 17 both depend on. Q3 2026 closes on 2026-09-30.
  • A cyclical drawdown in the bear case. No CPKC financial data before FY2012 was used, so the 2008-09 freight recession is absent from the reference material, and the bear case compounds ton-miles at −0.4% a year without a single year of cyclical volume decline in it.
  • Liability insurance. CPKC's per-occurrence limit, retention and annual premium are undisclosed, against a peer that exhausted an entire tower on one derailment.
  • The 2027 labour round. Compensation and benefits is 17.1% of revenue, the Teamsters agreements expire 2027-12-31, and the model assumes 3.0% a year thereafter with a 40bp bear delta, with no reference to recent Canadian rail arbitration awards or to the rate in the sixteen U.S. agreements ratified in January 2026.
  • Casualty expense in isolation. The CFO bundled it with stock-based and incentive compensation at about 150 basis points in Q2 2026, and whether a specific incident drove the first-half increase is not stated.
  • Contract terms on the concentrated channels. Duration and rate-reset terms for the Canpotex, K+S and Elk Valley Resources hauls, which together route more than 10% of revenue, are not described anywhere. The Q1 2026 call said only that Canpotex was "fully committed through the first half of the year".
  • Export terminal capacity. Grain, potash, coal and international intermodal are 40.5% of FY2025 revenue and all terminate at third-party facilities at Vancouver, Thunder Bay, Saint John, Montréal, Portland or Lázaro Cárdenas. The conclusion that supply is constrained at the origin was tested on the origin side only.
  • Automotive customers and plants. The driver stops at Mexican light-vehicle assembly on CPKC-served plants and an aggregate export figure, on 8.7% of revenue earning the highest yield in the book. AMIA and INEGI publish monthly production by manufacturer and plant.
  • Post-2027 industry structure. If UP–NS is approved, whether CPKC is an acquirer, a target or neither is not addressed by any disclosure. This management bid for Norfolk Southern in 2015 and bought KCS in 2021, and CN has already signed access terms with UP.
  • Line-level cost. Gross ton-miles, train-miles and switch events by commodity line do not exist in any CPKC disclosure, which is why every line margin in Section 1 is a banded estimate. The STB Uniform Rail Costing System and the Carload Waybill Sample would constrain it for the U.S. portion of the network.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Eleven decks from October 2014 to September 2026, 523 rendered slides. The August and September 2026 investor presentations differ only in the cover date and two footnote references, so the September copy is used. What the decks add beyond the filings and transcripts:

  • Commodity sub-splits the 10-K renders only as images. Item 1 of the FY2025 10-K introduces each split with "The following chart shows the percentage…" and then renders it as a picture, so the percentages are absent from the text layer. Slides 23 to 32 of the September 2026 deck supply them on a 2025 freight-revenue basis: grain 50% Canadian and 50% U.S. with Canadian grain 68% regulated; coal 61% Canadian; metals and minerals 37% steel, 33% mines and aggregates, 20% food and consumer, 10% frac sand; automotive 41% Mexico-origin finished vehicles; domestic intermodal 70% Canada and 23% cross-border; international intermodal 65% Vancouver, 13% Lázaro Cárdenas, 10% Montreal, 8% Saint John. These bound the regulated share of revenue at about 7% and the Mexican-origin automotive book at about 4% (§1, §3, §4).
  • Geographic mix of freight revenue. Slide 8 splits 2025 freight revenue into 41% cross-border, 33% domestic and 26% global, with Canada-to-Mexico at 1% and Mexico-to-Canada at 2%. The corridor the merger was built around is a low single-digit share of revenue today, while the border friction that makes it work is also what delays autonomous trucking on 41% of the book (§4, §6).
  • The synergy commitment in its original unit. Slide 6 of the 2021-09-16 deck states US$1bn of annualised EBITDA synergies within three years of closing, split US$820m from revenue and market opportunities and US$180m from cost and efficiency, with a footnote that the estimates are in U.S. dollars, and records the escalation from US$600m to US$780m to US$1bn before announcement. Every figure reported since 2024 is Canadian-dollar revenue (§8, §11).
  • The only running synergy tracker in the deck set. Slide 91 of the 2023 Investor Day reports US$240m of annualised actuals against about US$950m of line of sight, two and a half months after the control date. That is the most recent synergy total in any archived deck; later decks refer to realisation without a number (§11).
  • A US$5bn revenue opportunity pipeline with no date attached. Slide 26 of the 2023 Investor Day builds it from US$1,500m of industrial development and nearshoring, US$1,400m of truck-to-rail, US$1,100m of other self-help and US$925m of rail-to-rail, against segment-level "secured and line of sight" figures of US$800m for intermodal and automotive and US$1,125m for merchandise and energy. No completion date or conversion rate appears in any later deck (§6).
  • The truck-competitiveness proof point. Slide 43 of the 2023 deck puts San Luis Potosí to Chicago at 3.9 days actual on MMX 180/181 against 4.0 days by single-driver truck, 5.0 days advertised and 6.8 days by the next-closest interchange rail option (§2, §4).
  • Named share positions the 10-K does not give. The 2018 deck states CPKC moves 85% of Canadian export metallurgical coal and ships 70% of North American potash with direct access to all mines; the September 2026 deck states access to 25 automotive production facilities including 90% of Mexican assembly plants, a 24-hour Laredo rail crossing against 16 hours for trucks, and a 200-mile advantage on East Coast international intermodal into Montreal, Toronto and Chicago (§3, §4).
  • The 2024–2028 target block has not moved while four of its assumptions have. Slide 22 of the September 2026 deck repeats the June 2023 targets unchanged, with displayed assumptions of C$1.35 per U.S. dollar, US$4.15 diesel, C$330–370m of pension recovery and a 25.5% tax rate. The footnote beneath conceded two changes in October 2025 and four by August 2026. The pension line is the largest: the 2026 outlook assumes C$441m against the plan's C$330–370m, C$71–111m of pre-tax non-operating income inside a year guided to low double-digit earnings growth (§8, §14).
  • The ROIC ambition moved down between Investor Days without the arithmetic being stated. The 2018 deck asks for more than 15% adjusted return on invested capital; the 2023 deck claims more than 16% achieved for 2018–2022 and then asks only for a return to double digits. The KCS purchase price entering invested capital is the reason and no deck says so (§3, §8, §10).
  • A delivery claim that reports a shortfall. Slide 115 of the 2023 Investor Day, headed "Revisiting 2018 — Delivered On Our Commitments", lists high single-digit core adjusted EPS growth for 2018–2022, below the double-digit EPS growth CAGR the 2018 deck had targeted (§9).
  • Land presented two ways, twelve years apart. The 2014 deck devotes nine slides to real estate as a monetisation programme with more than US$1bn of gross sale value in surplus undeveloped land and more than C$100m a year of ancillary revenue within three to five years. From 2018 the same land is capacity to be held, reaching more than 6,000 developable acres in the 2023 deck. Schiller Park appears in both eras, as a 75-acre surplus site to be divested and as a 75-acre transload facility. FY2025 non-freight revenue, which includes leasing and subsurface rights, was C$302m and declined 7% (§10).
  • The safety series and the current-year run-rate point in opposite directions. Slide 20 of the September 2026 deck claims a third consecutive year of Class I leadership on FRA train accident frequency on a 2020–2025 series of 1.72, 1.72, 1.45, 0.99, 1.01 and 0.85. Slide 24 of the Q2 2026 deck, published five weeks earlier, shows year-to-date 2026 train accident frequency of 0.93 against 0.68 and personal injuries of 0.94 against 0.85. Both are accurate on their own terms and only the annual series appears in the positioning deck (§2, §13).
  • Two technology items that appear in no 10-K. Hyion Technologies, a joint venture with CSX Transportation to develop low-horsepower hydrogen fuel-cell-battery locomotives, is disclosed on slide 22 of the Q2 2026 deck; the same slide reports more than 1,100 biofuel fuelling events consuming about 10.2 million litres of B20 in British Columbia during 2025 (§2).
  • The Mexico Task Force result. Slide 5 of the Q3 2023 deck reports that ten weeks after inception CPKC de México car miles per car day improved 31%, locomotive productivity 10%, terminal dwell 14% and network speed 22%, in the same deck that cut 2023 earnings guidance to flat-to-slightly-positive (§9).
  • Volume since the merger with the coal drag separated. Slide 10 of the Q2 2026 deck gives cumulative second-quarter ton-mile growth of 17% from 2023 to 2026, and 22% excluding coal (§6).

Key slides

Appendix B — Web source excerpts

Ordered by first appearance in the body. All pages accessed 2026-09-21 unless noted.

1. Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada, Outlook for Principal Field Crops, 2025-12-17 — supports the 2025 Canadian crop record in §1 and §6. agriculture.canada.ca. The document, which incorporates the November 2025 Statistics Canada Field Crop Survey, gives total principal field crop production of 107.0 Mt for 2025, up 10.4% year over year and 16.2% above the 2020–2024 average of 92.1 Mt, against a prior record of 100.1 Mt in 2020, with western Canada 23% above its five-year average. The equivalent Statistics Canada Daily release of 2025-12-04 gives crop-by-crop figures of wheat 40.0 Mt and canola 21.8 Mt without a combined total.

2. Trans Mountain full utilisation — supports the pipeline-substitution mechanism in §1 and §6. hydrocarbonprocessing.com. The page reports the Trans Mountain system reaching full utilisation of its 890,000 bbl/d capacity in June 2026, after running at about 84% in summer 2025.

3. Canada Energy Regulator, crude by rail at a 13-year low — supports the crude-by-rail decline in §1 and §6. cer-rec.gc.ca. Canadian crude-by-rail exports were 1.8% of total Canadian crude exports in 2025, down from 2.1% in 2024, and have levelled at roughly 80,000 bbl/d since Trans Mountain started in spring 2024.

4. Canadian Transportation Agency, maximum grain revenue entitlements for crop year 2024-2025, 2025-12-19 — supports the regulated-grain figures in §1 and §18. canada.ca. CPKC's regulated grain revenue of $1,066,938,687 exceeded its entitlement of $1,064,278,437 by $2,660,250, with a 5% penalty of $133,012 payable to the Western Grains Research Foundation; CN's revenue of $1,454,604,793 was $5,913,453 below its entitlement of $1,460,518,246.

5. CPKC crop-year grain record, 2026-08-04 — supports the HEP tonnage ceiling in §2. prnewswire.com: "This new record annual volume exceeded the previous record set in the 2020-2021 crop year by approximately 72,500 metric tonnes." Total 2025-2026 movement was 30.66 million metric tonnes.

6. Gibson Energy and USD joint venture, Hardisty diluent recovery unit — supports the DRUbit contract structure in §2. usdg.com. The terminal page describes the Hardisty diluent recovery unit as a Gibson Energy and US Development Group joint venture with a 10-year, 50,000 bbl/d ConocoPhillips capacity agreement, designed to expand in 50,000 bbl/d increments.

7. Progressive Railroading, cold wheel technology — supports the Canadian regulatory exemption in §2. progressiverailroading.com. The article records the 2011 federal exemption applying cold wheel in place of manual air-brake inspection on CP's captive coal fleet, its 2018 extension to the grain, sulphur and potash fleets, air-brake failures down 50% since 2019, 2,600 more cars tested annually than manual inspection reached, and two FRA waivers sought for intermodal cars in the United States.

CPKC Technology and Innovation factsheet — supports the inspection-portal count and specification in §2. cpkcr.com: "This TIPS wayside detection system, located on our Maple Creek, Sask. subdivision, is equipped with over 35 cameras, providing a 360 view, and can scan trains in real-time at track speed generating 72 images per car and 100 GB of data per train… this is one of two TIPS along the Canadian CPKC network. Two additional RIPs are located along the borders in Mexico."
